The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Sunday that it has been preparing for the expected entry of Super Typhoon Champi into the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) this week.
In a news release, the agency said that as of 6 a.m., there are 4,571,390 family food packs prepositioned in its relief warehouses nationwide.
Meanwhile, 344,942 non-food items and 204,745 ready-to-eat food packs are also in stock.

"Sa pamamagitan po ng ating strategic hubs at warehouses, pinapanatili nating active ang supply chain para agad-agad nating maipahatid ang kinakailangang augmentation support kung sakali man na manghingi ng assistance ang mga komunidad na maaaring maapektuhan," DSWD Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said.

(Through our strategic hubs and warehouses, we are keeping the supply chain active so that we can immediately deliver necessary augmentation support should communities likely to be affected request assistance.)

Dumlao added that major production hubs are producing family food packs non-stop and that the agency's intensified disaster preparations align with the President's directive to maintain sufficient national stockpiles and ensure the fast delivery of relief assistance.

DSWD said it is continuing to monitor weather updates from the state weather bureau PAGASA, as the super typhoon could affect Northern Luzon, Cagayan Valley, and the northern portion of Ilocos Region toward the end of the week.

The DSWD said it is closely monitoring PAGASA weather updates on Champi, which is expected to impact Northern Luzon, Cagayan Valley, and the northern part of the Ilocos Region toward the end of the week.

articles.title: Angat Dam water level inches up amid strong El Niño
articles.summary: Angat Dam's water level rose by four centimeters to 209.51 meters on Sunday, just below its 210-meter normal high water level.

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 3:16pm
Receding waters of Angat Dam were seen on June 24, 2026, as its level continues to drop due to lack of rainfall.
STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — Angat Dam's water level rose slightly on Sunday, October 18, even as strong to very strong El Niño conditions persist in the tropical Pacific.
PAGASA recorded Angat Dam at 209.51 meters as of 8 a.m., up four centimeters from 209.47 meters on Saturday. The level remains just 0.49 meters below its normal high water level of 210 meters.

Angat Dam in Bulacan is the main source of water for the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System service area, supplying around 90% of its water requirements. Its operating zone extends down to 180 meters, below which the reservoir enters the drought zone.
PAGASA also recorded the following reservoir levels Sunday:

items: Ambuklao Dam: 751.06 meters
Binga Dam: 573.44 meters
Caliraya Dam: 286.30 meters
Ipo Dam: 100.77 meters
La Mesa Dam: 79.44 meters
Magat Dam: 191.88 meters
Pantabangan Dam: 209.75 meters
San Roque Dam: 283.54 meters

blocks.text: PAGASA said a strong to very strong El Niño is currently present in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue through the first half of 2027, possibly peaking before the end of 2026.
El Niño increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall, dry spells and drought, but PAGASA stressed that rain may still occur due to tropical cyclones and other weather systems.
For Sunday, the weather bureau forecast scattered rains and thunderstorms over parts of the country due to the easterlies, with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms possible elsewhere.

articles.title: ‘Many family stories’: Tim Winton’s Cloudstreet takes out ABC radio poll of top 100 Australian books
articles.summary:
Markus Zusak’s novel The Book Thief secures second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe rounds out podium dominated by men

Cloudstreet, Tim Winton’s sprawling Australian family…

blocks.text: Cloudstreet, Tim Winton’s sprawling Australian family epic, has been voted Australia’s favourite book in a poll run by ABC Radio National.
The broadcaster announced over the weekend the results of a nationwide poll to determine a list of readers’ top 100 Australian books.
Markus Zusak’s 2005 novel The Book Thief took second place, while Trent Dalton’s Boy Swallows Universe came in third.

First published in 1991, Cloudstreet follows two working-class Australian families, the Lambs and the Pickles, over their 20 years living together in an old rambling house called Cloudstreet, in postwar Perth.

The story – Winton’s fifth novel and ninth book – won a swathe of awards upon publication, including the Miles Franklin in 1992, and has been a staple of Australian English literature classes for decades. It’s sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Australia alone.

blocks.caption: Author Tim Winton in 2024. Photograph: Adam Ferguson

blocks.text: Cloudstreet has topped previous polls on Australian books, including one by the Australian Society of Authors surveying writers on their favourites in 2003, and a subsequent poll run by the ABC the same year, surveying the public. Winton’s novel appeared in a 2019 BBC list of “100 novels that shaped our world”.
The final top 100 in this year’s ABC Radio National poll included adult fiction, nonfiction, young adult fiction, children’s picture books, history and cookbooks.

The Australian Women’s Weekly Children’s Birthday Cake Book made it into the top 50 (at No 22), while Stephanie Alexander’s The Cook’s Companion came in at number 56. RecipeTin Eats: Dinner by Nagi Maehashi made the cut at 96.

Authors Helen Garner, Melissa Lucashenko, Geraldine Brooks, Anna Funder, Peter Carey and Hannah Kent all had multiple books in Sunday’s top 100. Books by children’s authors Alison Lester, Paul Jennings, Mem Fox, Jeannie Baker and Ruth Park appeared in the final 100.

The earliest published work was For the Term of His Natural Life by Marcus Clarke from 1874 (No 80). The most recent were Sally Hepworth’s Mad Mabel and Charlotte McConaghy’s Wild Dark Shore, both published in 2025.

Kate Evans, the host of ABC Radio National’s literary show The Bookshelf, said the list included “audacious literary fiction to historical accounts of who we’ve been and how we might understand all that complicated past, to joyful children’s books, Indigenous stories of both pain and humour, and many, many family stories”.
“This list defies any glib conclusions about how we read – and surely that’s the point,” Evans said.

articles.title: PCG, PSA sign data-sharing deal
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) have signed a data-sharing agreement to simplify the process of obtaining civil registry documents for personnel seeking…

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 3:13pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) have signed a data-sharing agreement to simplify the process of obtaining civil registry documents for personnel seeking benefits and other services.
The agreement allows the PCG to digitally verify PSA civil registry records for recruitment, pension claims, retirement benefits and other personnel-related transactions.

“Under the agreement, the PCG will be able to verify civil registry records maintained by the PSA for recruitment, retirement benefits, pension claims, and other personnel-related transactions,” the PCG said in a statement.

“The agreement also enables the digital processing of requests for civil registry documents, eliminating the need for PCG personnel and other concerned individuals to visit PSA service outlets in person,” it added.
The partnership aims to expedite processing and make essential government services more accessible to PCG personnel, retirees, pensioners and their dependents.

“It asks a simple question: when two institutions can work together to ease a person's burden, why should that burden remain on the person? Coordination is our responsibility. Service is our obligation. Dignity must be what every Filipino experiences when they come to government for help,” said PCG Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: 34 OFWs from Riyadh to arrive in Manila amid flight disruptions
articles.summary: The first batch of 34 OFWs being repatriated from Riyadh is set to arrive in Manila on Monday, October 19.

blocks.text: October 18, 2026 | 3:06pm
OWWA officials with the 34 OFWs expected to return to the Philippines.
OWWA / Released

MANILA, Philippines — The first batch of 34 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is set to arrive in the Philippines on Monday, October 19, as the government repatriates workers affected by regional tensions and flight disruptions.
In a statement Sunday, October 18, the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) said the 34 Filipinos are part of a broader repatriation operation covering 349 OFWs.
Of the total, 249 already have confirmed flight bookings, while arrangements are still being finalized for the remaining 100 workers.

The repatriation follows a series of drone and missile attacks targeting facilities and airports across Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The attacks have led to flight cancellations and delays.
Because of the disruptions, OWWA Riyadh, the Migrant Workers Office and the Philippine Embassy in Saudi Arabia arranged alternative routes through Al Qassim and Dammam for affected workers.

The first group of 34 traveled by land from Riyadh to Al Qassim Airport before boarding Qatar Airways flight QR 1197 to Doha. They will then take flight QR 934 to Manila and are expected to arrive at Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 on Monday morning.

Upon their arrival, OWWA's Repatriation and Assistance Division will provide airport assistance, temporary shelter when needed and domestic transportation for workers returning to their respective provinces.

articles.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
articles.summary: Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

image.caption: Babis has been described as 'Trumpist' in his outlookImage: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.
The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.
What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.
The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.
Babis called the result "catastrophic."
"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.
That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.
Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform
His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.
Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

articles.title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
articles.summary:
A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarch

When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s…

blocks.text: When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.
Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.
But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.
Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

blocks.caption: Bayo Randle, Bonetta’s great-great-grandson, is a barrister in London. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.
Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.
Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

blocks.caption: The book by Henry B Lovejoy. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.
Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.
Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

blocks.caption: Bonetta was a famous figure in 19th-century England. Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”

Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.

For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.

“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.

Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.
Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.

Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.

“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.

“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

articles.title: Condé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled out
articles.summary:
Magazine group points to restructuring bill but says it ‘remains profitable in the UK for another year’

Profits at Condé Nast’s UK arm slumped by more than a third last year, according to…

blocks.text: Profits at Condé Nast’s UK arm slumped by more than a third last year, according to figures published shortly after the billionaire family that owns the luxury magazine group and titles from Vogue to GQ ruled out a sale.

The publisher, which enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of its UK headquarters Vogue House in London, saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items tumble 36% from £28m that year to nearly £18m last year.

Revenues generated in the UK fell 7% from £75.9m to £70.6m, newly filed accounts showed. However, an 18% increase in international revenues, to £29.7m, helped keep the company’s total revenues almost flat, at £100m.

“Condé Nast remains profitable in the UK for another year,” a spokesperson for the publisher said. “The change in the exact level of profit reflects a period of planned investment in customised client solutions.”
Restructuring costs at the company, which publishes glossy titles and brands including Vanity Fair, House & Garden and Tatler, more than doubled year on year, from £1.9m to £4.3m.

Condé Nast said the latest restructuring charge was “primarily due to severance costs”. Despite the hefty restructuring bill, staff numbers remained almost flat, dipping from 466 to 461 between 2024 and last year.

“There were no large restructures in the UK business in 2025. There were isolated instances of redundancy, but headcount remained flat as hiring continued across the business,” the spokesperson said. “In addition, there have been changes to the pension scheme projections and wage inflation, which also impacted profit for this year.”

blocks.caption: Condé Nast had enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of Vogue House in Hanover Square, London. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Last week, Steven Newhouse, the chair of the Newhouse family holding company Advance that controls Condé Nast, ruled out a sale of the publishing giant. There had been speculation that the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, who owns the Washington Post, could buy the business.
Newhouse made the comment after the abrupt departure of the chief executive Roger Lynch, hired in 2019 to turn around the business, to become the boss of the toymaker Mattel.

“Maybe for a certain class of non-media owner, there’s a prestige to owning media properties,” he told the Financial Times. “But we’ve been a media owner for 100 years. So we’re not in it for the glamour.”

Earlier this year, Lynch described the introduction of Google’s AI Summaries – which often negate the need to click through to source material – as “another sort of death blow” to the way consumers have traditionally searched online and reached media outlets. He said Google searches were “no longer a meaningful driver” of Condé Nast’s business, accounting for only about a quarter of visits to its websites last year.
after newsletter promotion
Globally, seven of Condé Nast’s largest brands – Vogue, GQ, the New Yorker, Wired, Vanity Fair, Architectural Digest and Condé Nast Traveler – account for 85% of the company’s revenues.
Newsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of total revenues, with advertising and “other services” accounting for about 86%.

The publisher’s accounts filed at Companies House show that the highest-paid director - Natalia Gamero del Castillo Calleja, the company’s most senior executive outside the US who resigned last August - took home more than £1.3m.
Earlier this year, Condé Nast announced plans to shutter Self, its women’s health magazine, after 47 years.

articles.title: Lean Alejandro and climate justice: Why Lidy Nacpil now believes in living for a cause
articles.summary: A key lesson from our time as Martial Law babies is top of mind for Lidy in the battle for climate justice: You have to keep pushing — even when the odds seem overwhelming.

blocks.text: The devastating floods in Thailand and Nepal turned the spotlight on a familiar name for those of us who lived through Martial Law and dictatorship.

Lidy Nacpil was one of the leaders who fought the Marcos regime, a cause she and many from our generation were ready to die for. Now she’s a leader in the global battle against climate change, when the romance of dying for a cause has been overshadowed by the pressing need to stick around as long as possible for a struggle for future generations.

“Those who contributed the least to global emissions continue to shoulder the heaviest costs without prospects for a resilient future,” she said in an essay co-written with two prominent climate activists from Europe and Africa.
For Lidy, the stakes are higher than half a century ago when we faced off with the Marcos regime. We didn’t expect to live long back then. Dying young was possible.

We grew up under a dictatorship so brutal and with so little respect for life that many of us from the Martial Law generation believed that if we want to help end it, we would have to give up a lot for the fight — including our lives.

For Lidy, that became real on September 19, 1987. What was painfully ironic was that the dictatorship had already been overthrown then. But the fascists were still around and there were still forces who shared the dictator’s disdain for democracy and who targeted those who were fighting to preserve and expand it — like her husband, Lean Alejandro.
On that day, Lidy returned home to find the sitter of their 6-month-old daughter Rusan waiting for her at the door. She said Lean had been ambushed.

“My first thought was that she said ‘ambush’ So I was really hoping that it did not mean he was dead. So I said, ‘Where was he taken?’ I was so afraid of asking point blank: ‘Buhay pa ba? Is he still alive?’”
But the sitter confirmed her worst fear. Lean was dead.

Lean had just led a press conference before the attack to share plans for the upcoming 15th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law. He and several companions were about to drive into their office on Rosal Street in Cubao, when a van pulled up next to the car. Then the assassins opened fire.

Rosal Street is about a mile away from our house in Cubao. I actually remember hearing the shots, though I did not think much about it initially. Only an hour later did I realize its significance when a friend called and said she heard a radio report about the ambush.

I drove to the office which had been abandoned by the time I arrived. There was blood on the driveway. The staff, including friends of mine, had retreated to a nearby office of a major human rights coalition in New Manila.
We were in shock. A brilliant leader, the most inspiring symbol of the Martial Law generation, was gone.

Friends and family joined Lidy at the morgue for what she recalls as “a nightmare into the night.” Lean’s face was shattered in the attack. “What I did was not look at where he was badly damaged and just concentrated on looking at parts of his body and his face that were intact,” she said. “My memories of that day are still vivid. I don’t think I’ll ever forget.”

I last saw Lidy in person in 2007 when we commemorated Lean’s 20th death anniversary in Quezon City. By then, her activism had expanded in scope, focused not only on social justice and human rights issues in the Philippines, but also on a grim global concern: climate change.

In 2012, when I posted a Facebook note celebrating Barack Obama’s reelection despite misgivings about some of his policies, Lidy posted a comment: “Boying, hope he will have a far, far better position on climate change and US cuts on its emissions than he took during his first term.”

When we talked four years ago for my series on Martial Law Babies, the urgency of the climate change battle clearly informed her own updated view of activism — and the sacrifices one must be willing to make in the fight for change. (READ: The Martial Law babies’ turn)

We were in our late 20s when Lean was assassinated nearly 40 years ago. Most of us are now in our late 50s or early 60s. When we were younger, being prepared to die for the cause, for the struggle against dictatorship was a given. But things are different now, Lidy told me.
“The sacrifices and what we are willing to give up, nag iiba iba iyan (it changes),” Lidy said. “At that time for us, the biggest is you were willing to risk your life.”

“The challenge for me today is: you have to live long because there’s so much to do — and to pass on. We cannot recklessly risk our lives today. That’s not what is being asked for. The times are different. The needs are different.”

blocks.caption: Lean Alejandro and climate justice: Why Lidy Nacpil now believes in living for a cause

blocks.text: Lidy was a high school freshman at UP High when Martial Law was declared in September 1972. After a long break from school after Marcos seized power, she returned to a campus where there were “whispers” of students and teachers who had been arrested. But she had been vaguely aware of the protests and the unrest. She and her schoolmates didn’t have a clear idea of what was going on.
“That’s why we were called Martial Law babies. We were just babies, not literally in age but in consciousness.”
Although she would later be known as a UP student leader, it was actually through her church and groups like the Student Christian Movement that she became exposed to political activism.

In fact, she was initially unimpressed with the first student activists she encountered in Diliman. “I used to see small groups of students marching down the corridors of Palma Hall, sloganeering. I used to think, ‘Ano ba naman iyan, ang babaw. Paano mo mababago ang lipunan kung nagsisigaw ka lang diyan? (It was shallow. How will you change society by just yelling slogans?).”
She laughed at the memory, adding, “If that’s all we were going to do as students, do marches and shout slogans, I wasn’t interested. I was looking for something deeper and more profound.”
Eventually, she found it.

The marches and the slogans turned out to be just one part of a broader and more dynamic activist movement that was at that time starting to push back against the dictatorship. And these efforts, the years of testing the limits and pushing back against the regime — which had led to arrests and even the death of Philippine Collegian editor Ditto Sarmiento — eventually produced victories. By the time Lidy entered UP Diliman, students, after years of struggle, had reclaimed their right to elect their own student councils and other campus rights.
It was around that time that she met Lean. They would later share a scary experience — though one that they would later talk about lightheartedly.

It happened in 1980 when Lidy and Lean joined a major student demonstration at Liwasang Bonifacio. The rally was violently dispersed. “I fell during the dispersal. I vaguely remember someone helping me get up and then I ran.”

She didn’t see and had no idea who helped her up. But Lean later told her that it was him — and he actually paid a price for it. “I was about to get hit with a truncheon when he blocked it with his hand.”

Lean was wearing a Rado watch which got smashed in this act of chivalry. “His father had given it to him so it was valuable. Kaya sabi niya, ‘Ikaw ang dahilan kung bakit nabasag. (You’re the reason it got smashed.).”
Remembering that made Lidy laugh.

I still fondly remember Lean as a brilliant, inspiring activist — intelligent, articulate, charismatic. He was a young leader brimming with confidence who could give a firebrand speech at a rally at Mendiola Bridge and also engage in serious political discussions with established political figures like Lorenzo Tañada and Jose “Pepe” Diokno.

He was also a humble, patient young leader who I saw several times up close. During a rally shortly after the Aquino assassination, when he was not yet a nationally known figure, I saw Lean defuse a situation in the crowd where some impatient protesters started throwing little stones at other protesters who decided to stand up to see what was going on at the main stage.
“Huwag po. Magkakainitan lang po tayo niyan. (Sir, please don’t do that. It will just make things worse.),” Lean said calmly, successfully convincing the irritated rallyists to settle down.

I also remember Lean for his quirks and unorthodox style. He used to walk around Diliman in faded jeans and flip flops. He was known as a computer geek and an avid fan of chess, The Lord of the Rings, and Fiddler on the Roof.
Like many of us back then, he was a chain smoker — perhaps because many of us didn’t expect to lead long lives. So why not smoke our lungs away. We were prepared to go all in so to speak.

In fact, Lean famously said: “The line of fire is the place of honor.” The day he was assassinated, Lean was reading Antonio Gramsci, the Italian revolutionary who is also famous for the quote, “The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born.”
For Lidy, it is the first sentence of what Gramsci said that truly resonates more than 30 years later. The world indeed is dying — and there is much to be done.

Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement about 15 years ago. As one of the leaders of the Asian People’s Movement on Debt and Development, she has emerged as one of Asia’s leading voices in the movement.
That fight has become harder.

When the UN Climate Change Conference was held in 2021 without the participation of countries in the Global South, she was among those who spoke out. “The conference has long been dominated by wealthy governments and corporate interests, thus it’s always an intense effort to raise the voices, perspectives and calls of people and communities, especially those from the Global South,” she said.

When the Nepal tragedy hit, Lidy spoke out in a Bangkok Post op-ed: “Declarations can no longer substitute for action, and excuses can no longer be allowed. Behind every discussion of temperature thresholds, emissions pathways and international obligations are communities losing lives, homes, livelihoods and ecosystems.”
It is a different kind of struggle — one that poses a host of unique tougher challenges.

“You’re fighting for things not to get worse in terms of the climate. On the other hand, you want to establish systems where there’s more equality and where people will have a better chance of a good livelihood. “
“The real impact of climate change can no longer be reversed. What we’re telling people is we cannot go back to the past. We’re working to prevent things from getting worse.”
It would be hard to imagine a time when there are no super typhoons, she said. There is, in a way, the element of making people fearful of what could happen.

“That’s not the easiest thing to do. Mas madaling sabihin sa tao, ‘Lumaban tayo dito para mawala iyan’ imbes na ‘Lumaban tayo para hindi lumala.’ (It’s easier to tell people, ‘Let’s fight to make this go away,’ instead of ‘Let’s fight so things don’t get worse.’)”

But today’s generation of climate change activists also are “blessed,” she said. Activists from earlier generations had laid the foundation for the fight — similar to the way our generation learned a lot from the experiences of earlier activists and leaders like Tañada and Diokno.

Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement a decade after the 1992 international conference which helped make clear the dangers the world faced and establish basic principles on how nations should respond.
“I was surprised and wondered how they were able to win progressive provisions and principles, because they are really helping us now.”

Her past as a Martial Law baby, and a veteran of the struggle that overthrew the Marcos dictatorship has also helped. A key lesson from our time as Martial Law babies is top of mind for Lidy in the battle for climate justice: You have to keep pushing — even when the odds seem overwhelming.

“From our experience in the fight during the dictatorship, you learn to widen and push the edges of these platforms and these opportunities. Hindi ka pwedeng magkasya doon sa ito lang iyong binigay sa iyo. (You must never settle and accept what they say they can offer you.) You push for more so you can have more space to raise your voices.

“The discipline we developed as activists in the Philippines was helpful. We were very broad-minded in terms of tactics, strategies, and alliance work… What we experienced during martial law, what we learned about struggle, about strategies and tactics, these are very useful in taking on all these global problems and fights and institutions and arenas.“

For example, she said, with movements in some countries, there is a dichotomy between “those who just believe in mobilizations, mass actions and radical slogans and those who just do policy advocacy and do the nitty gritty of negotiations.”

That’s not how she was trained as an activist. In a way, the lesson goes back to her initial reaction to UP activists, those who held loud marches in Diliman — which she subsequently realized were just one part of a broader and deeper movement. Marches and pickets were just as important as other tasks, from studying an issue to formulating a policy and position and engaging negotiations to achieve a goal.
“Para sa Pinoy, lahat yan kasama. (For Filipinos, that’s all combined.) Those are all needed.”

There’s another lesson Lidy shared and it’s related to how we all remember Lean. “Lean had extraordinary and outstanding traits,” she said. But in honoring his memory, we shouldn’t idealize who he was.

“Ang hirap kasing naghohold up tayo ng icons minsan kasi baka ma-frustrate lang. (Holding up people as icons is sometimes not helpful. It may just lead to frustration.) Not everybody can be a Lean Alejandro.”
And not everyone has to be a Lean Alejandro, she said. That’s a key lesson from the Martial Law generation. Many of us weren’t. But that didn’t matter.

“I think the most important story of our generation is that most of us were just your average youth. The thing that was extraordinary about us is that we rose to the occasion. We weren’t particularly more intelligent. Mas sharper pa nga sila ngayon e. (Young people today are even sharper.) The knowledge base is much larger now. The technology is there. They are faster in dealing with all the technology.
“But we rose to the occasion. We realized that we had more than ourselves to live for.”

And that’s what she hopes young Filipinos today will keep in mind, she said — that “they realize that they have to live for more than themselves. And that they rise to the occasion, whatever the occasion demands, whatever the times now demand from them. It doesn’t take extraordinary things. It’s your willingness and readiness and there are many ways that you can contribute.”
In a way, the idea of “giving your life” for the cause — “medyo abstract na. (It’s a bit abstract now.),” Lidy said. “That means many different things.”
“I want to last as long as it takes until there is a fresh resurgence of movements and struggles so we can pass on whatever knowledge and wisdom we gained from our experiences.” – Rappler.com
This essay is based on an article first published in 2022.

Benjamin Pimentel is the author of ‘U.G. An Underground Tale: The Life and Struggle of Edgar Jopson’ published by Anvil Publishing which just released the 2nd printing of the 3rd edition. He is also a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Royalties from ‘U.G.’ are donated to Bantayog ng Mga Bayani.

articles.title: India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
articles.summary: Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

image.caption: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was released a day after his detentionImage: Dinesh Joshi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.
The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.
The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."
"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.
Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.
In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."
"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."
What are the protests about?
All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.
Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.

Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.
The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.
The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP
Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".
BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.
Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."

"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.
India: Protesters jailed amid election row
Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday
Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.
Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.
The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.
"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

articles.title: Senate eyes resolution on Chinese Embassy's dare on persona non grata call vs ambassador - Ejercito
articles.summary: The Senate is considering to issue a resolution in response to the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines' challenge to declare Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 2:24pm
The Senate is considering to issue a resolution in response to the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines' challenge to declare Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday.

Ejercito described Jing Quan’s earlier statement as “very rude, very hostile, and very undeplomatic,” after the latter claimed that China would "easily win" if it resorted to force in the West Philippine Sea.

“Hintayin na lang natin ang plenary... Pinag-uusapan na kung magpapasa kami ng resolusyon ukol sa kanyang pananalita. Pero malamang, magkakaroon ng aksyon at resolusyon ang Senado ukol dito,” Ejercito told Super Radyo dzBB.
(Let us wait for the plenary session. We are already discussing whether to file a resolution regarding his remarks. But most likely, the Senate will take action and issue a resolution on the matter.)

On Saturday, the Chinese Embassy released a statement amid talks of possibly declaring Jung Quan persona non grata after his remarks were perceived by some lawmakers as “threats” against the Philippines.
"Some senators and house representatives are talking about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata. Is this threat or coercion?" the Chinese Embassy said in a social media post.
"But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING," it added.
Ejercito said Jing Quan should be replaced as Chinese ambassador, saying his remarks were already threatening in nature and only adds to the tension and conflict between the two countries.

“Maganda, dapat mapalitan na lang ito. Itong Chinese ambassador belongs to a group na talagang nag-i-instigate. Parang sinasadyang talaga nila 'yan at hindi 'yan nakatutulong sa ating pag-repair o pag-ayos sa relasyon [ng Pilipinas at China],” Ejercito said.

(It would be better if he were replaced. This Chinese ambassador belongs to a group that deliberately instigates tensions. It seems they are doing this on purpose, and it does not help repair or improve relations between the Philippines and China.)
“Dapat palitan 'yan ng Tsina, kung seryoso silang ayusin ang relasyon sa ating bansa,” he added.
(China should replace him if it is serious about improving relations with our country.)
Meanwhile, Senator Jinggoy Estrada urged caution against hastily declaring someone persona non grata.

“While I share the concern and indignation his words have stirred, we must protest strongly and demand respect, without closing the doors of dialogue. Walang magandang idudulot ang padalus-dalos na pagkilos bilang tugon sa mga sinabi ng Chinese envoy (taking hasty action in response to the Chinese envoy’s remarks will do no good)," Estrada said in a statement.
“Madaling sabihin ang pagdedeklara ng persona non grata, pero ang pananagutan sa magiging kahihinatnan nito ay hindi madaling pasanin,” he added.
(Declaring someone persona non grata is easy to say, but the responsibility for its consequences is not easy to bear.)

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: PH, US eye expanded cooperation on energy security
articles.summary: The Philippines and the United States are looking to expand their cooperation on energy security and diversify energy sources following a meeting in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 1:50pm
The Philippines and the United States are looking to expand their cooperation on energy security and diversify energy sources following a meeting in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15.
Department of Energy (DOE) Secretary Sharon Garin met with her US counterpart, Chris Wright, to discuss potential cooperation in liquefied natural gas (LNG), coal, geothermal and nuclear energy.
“Our priority is to ensure a secure, reliable, and affordable energy supply for Filipino families and businesses," Garin said in a statement.

Strengthening our partnership with the United States will help us diversify our energy sources, develop indigenous resources, and build the technical capabilities needed to support our long-term energy security,” she added.
The two countries are also exploring potential cooperation on strategic petroleum reserves, according to the DOE.
On nuclear energy, the officials discussed cooperation under the Philippines-US Agreement for Cooperation Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy, which took effect in 2024.

“Both sides discussed initiatives supporting the Philippines' preparations for nuclear power development, including the US Department of State's Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) program, which supports technical and institutional capacity-building for safe and responsible nuclear energy development,” the DOE said.

The officials also highlighted a US Trade and Development Agency-funded reverse trade mission aimed at connecting Philippine leaders and industry stakeholders with American nuclear technology suppliers and experts in financing, regulatory affairs and workforce training.

The meeting also covered opportunities to develop indigenous energy resources, particularly geothermal energy and natural hydrogen. The officials examined Koloma's local exploration efforts and how these could contribute to the Philippines' long-term energy mix, the DOE said.
The agency said it would continue pursuing international partnerships to strengthen the country's energy supply.

The government is also promoting the Philippines as a potential oil storage hub for Asia, with the DOE proposing to allow foreign countries to establish storage facilities in the country.--MCG, GMA News

articles.summary: As of Sunday morning, October 18, Super Typhoon Champi is located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon, still outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

blocks.text: CHAMPI. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Champi outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of October 18, 2026, 10:30 am.
PAGASA
As of Sunday morning, October 18, Super Typhoon Champi is located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon, still outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

items: Champi is expected to enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility as a super typhoon on Tuesday, October 20.
While landfall in the Philippines appears less likely, Champi may still affect parts of the country, especially extreme Northern Luzon.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – A tropical cyclone with the international name Champi is expected to enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Tuesday, October 20.
Champi had intensified from a typhoon into a super typhoon as of 2 am on Sunday, October 18, and it is projected to enter PAR as a super typhoon.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in an advisory that Champi was located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 10 am on Sunday.
The super typhoon is moving west at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h), while over the sea near the United States island territory of Guam.

Champi did not make landfall in Guam, but still lashed the island with heavy rain and damaging winds during its closest point of approach in the early hours of Sunday, according to Guam Homeland Security. Guam is just two hours ahead of Manila.
So far, Champi has maximum sustained winds of 185 km/h — the minimum threshold for classification as a super typhoon by PAGASA — and gustiness of up to 230 km/h.
The weather bureau sees Champi strengthening further and possibly reaching a peak intensity of 205 km/h before its entry into PAR, but it may start gradually weakening on Tuesday.
Once it enters PAR on Tuesday morning or afternoon, Champi will be given the local name Rosal. It would be the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October.
Champi only has a slim chance of making landfall in the Philippines, as it is more likely to head for Taiwan. Taiwan, located above the northernmost province of Batanes, is within PAR.
Although landfall is less likely in the country, PAGASA warned the public that Champi may still bring heavy rain to extreme Northern Luzon, or the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area.

The weather bureau might also raise tropical cyclone wind signals for the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and even parts of Bicol as early as Monday evening, October 19, or by Tuesday morning, since winds from Champi could reach these areas. The highest wind signal may be Signal No. 3 or 4.
PAGASA added that most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, are likely to experience gusty conditions beginning Tuesday or Wednesday, October 21.
Also on Tuesday, moderate to rough waters are expected in the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao.
Starting Wednesday, very rough, high, or very high waters may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon.

blocks.text: For now, the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies are the weather systems affecting the country on Sunday.
The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean.

The ITCZ is causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Zamboanga Peninsula, Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and Soccsksargen.
Meanwhile, the easterlies are bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to Quezon and Camarines Norte, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of the country.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com
